passage: In the small town, Jeevan's family ran a tea stall that opened at six, and he helped before school. Every night he stayed up late, first studying, then watching videos on his phone under the blanket. By morning his eyes burned. His friend Zubin, who helped at his uncle's shop across the road, noticed him yawning over the kettle. "You look like a ghost," Zubin said. Jeevan snapped at him, then apologised. He knew he was grumpy. His exams were near, and he'd been falling asleep during revision anyway. That week he tried studying straight after school, while his mind was fresh, and kept his phone near the kettle at night. By Friday he was still tired but not burning-eyed, and he laughed at Zubin's joke again.

qa.q: What time did the tea stall open?
qa.a: It opened at six.

qa.q: Why did Jeevan snap at Zubin and then apologise?
qa.a: Lack of sleep made him grumpy, and he quickly realised Zubin was only concerned, so he felt bad.

qa.q: What changes helped Jeevan, and why?
qa.a: Studying right after school used his fresh hours, and keeping the phone away at night cut the late viewing that stole his sleep.

qa.q: How might Jeevan's parents see the change by Friday?
qa.a: They might notice he is less grumpy and more helpful at the stall, even if he's still a bit tired.

grounding: It shows a teen managing early duties, late-night phone use and study load to improve sleep.

passage: In Copenhagen, Emil had rowing practice at six in the morning, three days a week. He was sixteen, and his body didn't want to sleep before midnight. He tried everything: warm milk, counting, lying still. Nothing worked, and he began to dread the alarm. His older sister, Dalia, a nursing student, found him on the sofa at 12:30 scrolling through clips. "Your brain's waiting for the next one," she said. "Teen body clocks run late anyway. The screen pushes it later." She suggested he read a paper book in dim light, leave the phone in the kitchen, and ask the coach if some sessions could move. The coach agreed to one later practice. Emil still yawned, but he stopped hating mornings quite so much.

qa.q: What time was Emil's rowing practice?
qa.a: It was at six in the morning, three days a week.

qa.q: Why did Emil begin to dread the alarm?
qa.a: He couldn't fall asleep before midnight, so early practice left him exhausted and he felt stuck between his body and his schedule.

qa.q: How did Dalia's suggestions address the problem?
qa.a: She explained that teen body clocks run late, then suggested reducing screens and talking to the coach, tackling both habits and schedule.

qa.q: How might the coach see Emil's request?
qa.a: The coach might understand that young rowers need sleep to train well and see moving one session as reasonable.

grounding: It shows a teen with a shifted body clock managing late-night screens and early commitments.

passage: At the girls' hostel in Pune, lights went off at ten-thirty, but Kalyani, sixteen, kept studying with her phone torch under the blanket. Then scrolling. She couldn't fall asleep before one anyway, her body just wasn't tired. In the morning she dragged herself to the six-thirty prayer assembly and dozed off in chemistry twice. Ritu, her roommate, watched this for a week. 'Your body clock's shifted, not broken,' she said. 'Mine too. But the phone makes it worse.' They made a deal: phones in the locker at eleven, heavy chapters before dinner, easy reading after. Kalyani also started walking in the courtyard in the morning sun. It took two weeks, but she stopped nodding off in chemistry.

qa.q: When did lights go off in the hostel?
qa.a: At ten-thirty.

qa.q: How did Kalyani seem to feel about her late nights at first?
qa.a: She felt stuck, since her body wasn't tired before one even though she was exhausted in the mornings.

qa.q: Which parts of Kalyani and Ritu's plan could other teens borrow?
qa.a: Putting phones away at night, moving heavy study earlier and getting morning sunlight.

qa.q: How might the chemistry teacher notice the change in Kalyani?
qa.a: The teacher would see her more alert and awake instead of dozing off in class.

grounding: Shows a teen in a hostel managing a shifted body clock, late-night phone use and study load.

passage:
Dear Bidisha di,
How's college? I have a sleep problem and you're the only one who won't lecture me.
This year my body just won't sleep before one at night. I lie there wide awake while Maa thinks I'm on my phone. Sometimes I am, okay. Then the alarm at six feels like a punch. I read that teen body clocks actually shift later, so it's not only laziness.
Here's what I'm trying: no phone in bed, it charges on the dressing table. Maths early in the evening, when my brain works. Opening the curtains the moment I wake up. On weekends I'm trying not to sleep till noon, which is TORTURE.
It's slightly better. Any tips from hostel life?
Nazia

qa.q: Where does Nazia's phone charge now?
qa.a: On the dressing table, not in bed.

qa.q: Why does Nazia call Bidisha di the only one who won't lecture?
qa.a: Nazia feels misunderstood at home, since Maa assumes it's only the phone, and trusts Bidisha di to listen.

qa.q: What is sensible about Nazia's plan?
qa.a: It works with a shifted body clock by moving hard study earlier, cutting phone use in bed and using morning light.

qa.q: How might Maa's view change if Maa read this letter?
qa.a: Maa might understand Nazia's late nights aren't only laziness and support Nazia's plan instead of blaming.

grounding: A teen writes about a shifted sleep clock, late-night use and study load, and a plan to manage them.

passage:
Dilnaz, you asked how I fixed my sleep in Class 12. Honestly, it was a mess.
I'd lie in bed at eleven, wide awake, and scroll until two. Then I'd drag myself up at six for tuition. By afternoon I was a zombie. I thought I was just lazy.
Our biology teacher said teenagers' body clocks actually shift later, so feeling awake at night is normal, but the phone makes it worse.
So I made changes. Phone charging in the kitchen from ten. Hard subjects in the afternoon when I was awake, not at midnight. Same wake-up time on Sundays, even though I hated it.
It took about three weeks. Now I'm Elizabeth, the girl who sleeps by eleven. My friends think it's hilarious.

qa.q: Where did Elizabeth's phone charge from ten?
qa.a: In the kitchen.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel before fixing the sleep routine?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt exhausted, like a zombie, and thought it was just laziness.

qa.q: Which changes helped Elizabeth, and why?
qa.a: Charging the phone outside the room, doing hard subjects in the afternoon and keeping the same wake-up time, which worked with her body clock.

qa.q: How do Elizabeth's friends see her new routine?
qa.a: They find it hilarious that she now sleeps by eleven.

grounding: A seventeen-year-old explains managing a shifted body clock, late-night phone use and study load.

passage:
I'm Kashish, Manoj's sister. In Class 11, Manoj, sixteen, started studying from ten at night till two in the morning, with his phone next to his books.
At breakfast he looked grey. He snapped at Mummy about the tea. He fell asleep on the bus and missed his stop twice.
One weekend he slept until one in the afternoon and still woke up tired.
Then, after he failed a chemistry test he'd studied all night for, I saw him make a timetable. Studying from four to eight in the evening. Lights off by 11:30. Phone outside his room.
The first week he complained a lot. By the third week he stopped looking grey. I don't know if he'll keep it up. But he laughed at breakfast yesterday.

qa.q: Until what time did Manoj used to study?
qa.a: Till two in the morning.

qa.q: How did Manoj seem to feel in the weeks of late-night study?
qa.a: He seemed exhausted and irritable, snapping at Mummy and falling asleep on the bus.

qa.q: What changes did Manoj make to his schedule, and why are they sensible?
qa.a: He studied from four to eight, switched lights off by 11:30 and kept the phone outside his room, giving him more sleep.

qa.q: How does Kashish see her brother's change?
qa.a: She notices he looks better and laughs again, though she isn't sure he'll keep it up.

grounding: A sister observes her brother manage late-night studying and sleep after a failed test.

passage:
Week one: Lalremsiami, fifteen, kept a sleep diary for her health project. Weekdays: asleep at 1 a.m., up at 6. Weekends: asleep at 3, up at noon. Joseph, her project partner, laughed. “You're living in two time zones.”
Week three: She tried one change: same wake-up time every day, even Saturday, 7:30. She hated Saturday. She was yawning at the breakfast table and cranky with her brother.
Week six: Her diary showed she was falling asleep by 11:30 most nights without trying. She had stopped needing three alarms. In the project presentation, she showed the chart and said, “I thought I was a night person. Maybe I was just jet-lagged every Monday.”
Joseph got the class to clap.

qa.q: What did Joseph say about Lalremsiami's sleep?
qa.a: “You're living in two time zones.”

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami feel about waking at 7:30 on Saturdays at first?
qa.a: She hated it and felt cranky and sleepy.

qa.q: What change helped Lalremsiami's sleep, and why?
qa.a: Keeping the same wake-up time every day, which let her body clock settle.

qa.q: How might Joseph feel about the project result?
qa.a: He probably feels impressed and pleased that the diary showed such a clear change.

grounding: Over six weeks a fifteen-year-old regulates her shifted sleep pattern with a consistent wake time.

passage:
Ojas, you're yawning at breakfast again. Sit. Let me tell you what happened to me at your age.
I was sixteen, studying for my Class 11 exams. I used to read till two in the morning by the lamp because the house was quiet then. Then I'd wake at six for school. By the third week, I fell asleep in the bus, missed my stop, and ended up at the depot.
Our neighbour, a nurse, saw me walking back. She said, "Teenagers' body clocks shift later, but you still need your hours. Study earlier, sleep earlier, even if it feels wrong."
I tried it. It felt strange for a week. Then my marks went up.
Your Deepika Maasi is telling you: put the phone down by eleven.

qa.q: Where did young Deepika end up after falling asleep in the bus?
qa.a: At the depot.

qa.q: What was young Deepika feeling when walking back from the depot?
qa.a: Deepika probably felt exhausted and embarrassed after missing the stop.

qa.q: What choice inside the story helped young Deepika's studies?
qa.a: Deepika chose to follow the nurse's advice to study earlier and sleep earlier, even though it felt strange at first.

qa.q: How might the neighbour nurse have seen young Deepika walking back?
qa.a: The nurse likely saw a tired teenager who needed kind, practical advice about sleep.

grounding: An aunt tells her nephew how she learned to manage her shifted body clock and study load.

passage:
Harsha's board exams started in six days, and the wedding next door had a DJ until midnight every night. Harsha lay awake with a pillow over his head.
His friend Baljeet texted at 12:30: "Can't sleep either. Want to revise on call?"
Harsha almost said yes. Then he remembered the headache from last week after three nights of this.
"No. I'm going to try earplugs and sleep. Revise at 7 a.m.?"
He found the earplugs his father used on trains, and turned his phone face down. It still took an hour to fall asleep.
At 7, he and Baljeet revised on call. His head felt clearer than it had all week.

qa.q: How many days were left before Harsha's board exams?
qa.a: Six days.

qa.q: What was Harsha feeling when he almost said yes to Baljeet?
qa.a: Harsha felt tempted and restless, unable to sleep with the noise.

qa.q: Which choice helped Harsha, and why?
qa.a: He chose sleep with earplugs and moved revision to the morning, which protected rest before exams.

qa.q: How might Baljeet be affected by Harsha's reply?
qa.a: Baljeet also gets a better plan and a clear morning revision session instead of a tired late-night one.

grounding: Amid wedding noise before exams, a teen protects his sleep and shifts study to the morning.

passage:
In their Mumbai flat, Kavitha had a pattern: homework till eleven, then chatting with Sabina till two, then alarm at six. She told herself her body just liked nights.
At school she dozed in chemistry and snapped at her mother at breakfast.
The school nurse, seeing her yawning, said, "Teens' body clocks do shift later. But your school starts at seven-thirty. The clock doesn't change that."
That evening, Kavitha texted Sabina: "New rule. Chat stops at 11:30."
Sabina replied, "Thank god. I'm dying."
The first nights were hard; Kavitha lay awake. But by the second week, she wasn't dozing in chemistry. She even laughed at breakfast.

qa.q: What time does Kavitha's school start?
qa.a: At seven-thirty.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling in the mornings before the change?
qa.a: Kavitha felt exhausted and irritable, snapping at her mother.

qa.q: What small step helped Kavitha get more sleep?
qa.a: Setting a clear end time for chatting with Sabina, even though the first nights were hard.

qa.q: How does Sabina see the new rule?
qa.a: Sabina is relieved, because she was also exhausted by the late chats.

grounding: A teen learns to manage a shifted body clock by setting a late-night chat limit.

passage:
"Leela, it's one o'clock."
"I know, Didi. I can't sleep anyway."
Vinita sat on the edge of the bed. "Is it the phone?"
"Partly. But even when I put it away, my brain wakes up at night. In the morning I'm a zombie."
"Mine did that at your age. Teenage body clock. Doesn't mean you should feed it."
"And I have two tests this week."
"So what do you usually do at night?"
"Revise. Then scroll. Then panic."
Vinita laughed. "Okay. What if you do the hardest revision right after school, when you're awake? Phone charges with me at eleven. And lights off by half past, even if you just lie there."
"Lying there is boring."
"Boring is the point."
Leela groaned, but she handed over her phone.

qa.q: What time does Vinita say it is?
qa.a: It's one o'clock.

qa.q: How does Leela feel about her sleep, and what shows it?
qa.a: Leela feels frustrated and tired, calling herself a zombie in the mornings and describing night-time panic.

qa.q: What plan did Vinita suggest, and why does it make sense?
qa.a: Hardest revision after school, phone charging with Vinita at eleven, and lights off by half past, so study moves earlier and the phone isn't there to keep Leela awake.

qa.q: How might Vinita feel finding Leela awake at one?
qa.a: Vinita probably feels concerned but understanding, remembering having the same trouble at that age.

grounding: Illustrates a teen and an older sister working out how to manage a shifted body clock, late-night use and study load.

passage:
Last year I was sleeping about five hours a night. I'd start maths at 10 p.m. because that's when I finally felt awake, then watch "just one" video, and wake up at 6:30 for the school bus feeling like I'd been hit.
I blamed myself for being lazy. Then my friend Gurpreet said her sister, a nurse, had told her teenagers' body clocks actually shift later. That made me feel less stupid, but it didn't fix the bus.
So I tried a few things. I moved maths to 5 p.m. I kept my phone in the living room after 10. On Sundays I didn't sleep till noon, just an hour extra, so Monday wasn't a disaster.
It took about two weeks. Now I'm mostly fine. I'm Yamini, and I still hate 6:30. But I'm not a zombie anymore.

qa.q: What time did Yamini move maths to?
qa.a: Yamini moved maths to 5 p.m.

qa.q: How did Yamini feel on hearing that teenagers' body clocks shift later?
qa.a: Yamini felt relieved and less stupid, no longer blaming laziness.

qa.q: Which of Yamini's changes seems most useful, and why?
qa.a: Moving hard study earlier and keeping the phone out after 10, because it works with the late body clock without losing sleep to scrolling.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet see Yamini's change?
qa.a: Gurpreet might feel glad that sharing what her sister said helped a friend stop blaming herself.

grounding: Shows a teen understanding a shifted body clock and adjusting study times and phone use.

passage:
Hostel health note. Rehana, residential nurse.
Yamini came to the sick room for the third time this month with a headache. Her temperature is normal. When I asked about sleep, she said she studies till 1 a.m. because "the corridor is quiet then", then scrolls for half an hour, and gets up at 6 for prayers and breakfast.
She said, "I can't concentrate in class, so I study more at night, so I'm tired in class." She laughed, but she looked worried.
We made a small plan together: study in the reading room from 7 to 10 while it's open, phone in the locker at 10:30, lights off by 11. She thought it wouldn't work because her body "doesn't feel sleepy" then. I said to give it two weeks.
I've told her house mother, and will see her again next Friday. If the headaches continue, I'll arrange for the doctor to see her.

qa.q: Until what time does Yamini study at night?
qa.a: She studies till 1 a.m. because the corridor is quiet then.

qa.q: What does Yamini's laugh while looking worried suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Yamini was anxious about her tiredness but trying to brush it off.

qa.q: What was sensible about Rehana's plan?
qa.a: It moved study into earlier, supported hours and set a phone and lights-off time, with a check-in and a doctor if the headaches continue.

qa.q: How might the house mother see her role now?
qa.a: The house mother may feel responsible for supporting the plan, like reminding Yamini at 10:30.

grounding: Illustrates a nurse helping a teen manage late-night study, phone use and a shifted body clock in a hostel.

passage:
Tuesday, 1:20 a.m.
Can't sleep again. I got into bed at eleven like Mum asked, but my brain switched on like a light. Scrolled till 12:30, then finished the physics worksheet under the blanket.
This morning at 6:30 I felt drugged. Fell asleep in first period. Manoj, my brother, found it hilarious and did an impression of me snoring at breakfast. Not funny.
Biology Miss said teens' body clocks shift later, so we're not lazy, just out of sync with school. That actually made me feel better.
New plan: phone charges in the kitchen from ten. Worksheets done before dinner, not after. Dim lamp and a novel in bed. Sunday no sleeping till noon, because that apparently makes Monday worse.
Manoj says it won't last. We'll see.
Elizabeth

qa.q: Where will the phone charge from ten?
qa.a: The phone charges in the kitchen from ten.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel after hearing what Biology Miss said about body clocks?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt relieved and less guilty, understanding the late nights weren't just laziness.

qa.q: Which parts of Elizabeth's plan are most likely to help, and why?
qa.a: Keeping the phone out of the bedroom and finishing homework before dinner, because they remove the two things that kept Elizabeth up past midnight.

qa.q: How does Manoj see his sibling's sleep problem?
qa.a: Manoj treats it as a joke, doing a snoring impression and doubting the plan will last.

grounding: Shows a teenager understanding a shifted body clock and planning around late-night phone use and study load.
